settings.name_in_paper: adversarial multi-armed bandit (bandit online decision problem) against adaptive adversary
settings.definition_quote: Assume that $c_1,c_2,\ldots\in [0,1]^n$ is a sequence of cost vectors. There are $n\geq 1$ experts. ... Then an adaptive adversary is a function $A:[0,1]^{n\times t-1}\times \{1\ldots n\}^{t-1}\to[0,1]^n$.

settings.name_in_paper: bandit with countably infinitely many arms/experts with prior weights, adaptive adversary
unmapped: countably infinite arm set (action_space finite_K used as closest unstructured option)
learner knows prior weights w^i summing to at most 1
settings.definition_quote: The adversary subsequently generates cost vectors $c_t\in[0,1]^\infty$, and at each time $t$ we have to select one index or expert $i$ and incur its cost $c_t^i$. We learn only the cost of the selected expert. As a prerequisite, we need that each of the infinitely many experts is associated with a prior weight $w^i$

algorithms.name: FPL using all observations with oracle sampling probabilities
FPL using all observations with Monte Carlo estimated sampling probabilities
bFPL for infinite expert class (entering times)

source.label: thMain
source.quote: Let $\gamma_t=\min\big\{1,t^{-\frac{1}{3}}\big(n\sqrt{\log n}\big)^{\frac{2}{3}}\big\}$ and $\eta_t=\frac{\gamma_t}{n^2} t^{-\frac{1}{3}}\big(n\sqrt{\log n}\big)^{\frac{2}{3}}$. Then, for any $T\geq(n\log n)^2$, each expert $i\in\{1\ldots n\}$, and \emph{any} adaptive assignment of the costs $c_1,c_2,\ldots$, bFPL satisfies the regret bound \Expect c\leqT\bfpl-c\leqT^i \leq 4\Big(Tn\sqrt{\log n}\Big)^{\frac{2}{3}}.

results.notes: Regret E[cost] - E[c^i_{1:T}] for each fixed expert i (max outside expectation), recorded as pseudo_regret. n = K. Rates do not depend on T, so anytime. Also holds in label-efficient setting.

source.label: thMain
source.quote: (For $T<(n\log n)^2$, the regret is clearly at most $(n\log n)^2$.)

results.notes: Trivial branch stated parenthetically in Theorem 2.

source.label: propHP
source.quote: For each $T\geq 1$ and $0\leq\delta\leq 1$, the actual costs of bFPL are bounded with probability at least $1-\delta$ by c\leqT\bfpl\leq\Expect c\leqT\bfpl+\sqrt{2T\log\tfrac{2}{\delta}}.

results.notes: Bound on deviation of actual cumulative cost above expected cost (Azuma), not itself a regret bound.

conditions: sampling probabilities P(I_t = i) provided by an oracle

source.label: thChati
source.quote: The algorithm FPL (\ref{eqFPL}), obtaining cost estimates according to (\ref{eq:chati}) and with learning rate $\eta_t=\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{2nt}}$ achieves a regret of at most \Expect c\leqT\fpl-c\leqT^i \leq 2\sqrt{2Tn\log n} for any i.

results.notes: Requires oracle access to FPL's selection probabilities (computationally infeasible per the paper). Holds against adaptive adversary via the paper's argument.

tuning: k = ceil(2 t^2 log(2 sqrt t)) Monte Carlo samples

source.quote: Let $\gamma_t=\frac{1}{2\sqrt t}$ be the exploration threshold. In each time step, after selecting one expert $i$, let FPL obtain an estimate $\hat p_t^i=\max\{\gamma_t,\tfrac{a^i(k)}{k}-\tfrac{\gamma_t^2}{\sqrt 2}\}$ ... by sampling the perturbed leader $k=\lceil2t^{2}\log(2\sqrt{t})\rceil$ times ... Then the algorithm FPL with learning rate $\eta_t=\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{2nt}}$ achieves a regret of at most \Expect c\leqT\fpl-c\leqT^i \leq 2\sqrt{2Tn\log n} +7\sqrt T

results.notes: O(t^2 log t) samples per step, polynomial time per round.

conditions: prior weights sum to at most 1

source.label: thInf
source.quote: Consider a bandit problem with countably many arms/experts, each expert $i$ having a prior weight $w^i$ such that the weights sum up to at most $1$. Then the above described bFPL variant with entering times ..., exploration rate $\gamma_t=t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$, and learning rate $\eta_t=t^{-\frac{3}{4}}$, satisfies the regret bound \Expect c\leqT\bfpl-c\leqT^i \leq O(...) for all $T\geq 1$, any adaptive assignment of the cost vectors and any reference expert $i$.

results.notes: Proof omitted in paper. Expression recorded as printed (log w^i, presumably meant log(1/w^i)).
